An interview is a formal conversation between two or more people, where one person asks questions and the other answers them, with a specific purpose in mind.

The key idea is that it is not just any casual chat — it has a goal, a structure, and usually takes place in a serious or professional setting.

In any interview, there are two sides:

  • The interviewer — the person who asks the questions. They are in control of the conversation and are trying to find out something.
  • The interviewee — the person who answers the questions. They are being assessed, studied, or heard.
What makes something an "interview" and not just a conversation?

Three things set an interview apart from a regular conversation:

  1. Purpose — There is always a clear reason for the interview. Someone wants to hire, select, investigate, or understand.
  2. Structure — Questions are usually prepared in advance, and the flow is deliberate.
  3. Asymmetry — One person holds the questions; the other holds the answers. It is not an equal back-and-forth like a normal discussion.

The word "interview" is used in several different situations:

1. Job interview
This is the most common use. When a company wants to hire someone, they call candidates for an interview. The employer asks questions to find out if the person has the right skills, experience, and personality for the job. The candidate answers to show why they are the best choice. The outcome is usually a decision — hired or not.

2. Journalism interview
A reporter or journalist conducts an interview with a public figure — a politician, a celebrity, a scientist, an author — to gather information for a news article, a magazine piece, or a TV/radio program. Here, the purpose is to inform the public.

3. Research or academic interview
Researchers sometimes interview people to gather data. For example, a psychologist might interview patients, or a historian might interview people who witnessed a historical event. The goal here is to collect personal accounts or opinions systematically.

4. Police or investigative interview
Law enforcement officers conduct interviews with witnesses, victims, or suspects to gather information about a crime. This is a formal, recorded conversation with legal implications.

5. Medical or clinical interview
A doctor sometimes conducts a clinical interview with a patient — asking about symptoms, history, and lifestyle — to diagnose or understand a health condition better.

6. University or college admission interview
Some educational institutions invite applicants for an interview before admitting them, to assess their suitability beyond grades and test scores.

An interview can happen in different formats:

  • In person — both people meet face to face, which is the traditional and most personal form.
  • Over the phone — a voice conversation, often used for an initial or screening interview.
  • Over video call — increasingly common, especially since remote work became widespread. It combines the personal feel of face-to-face with the convenience of distance.
  • Written or email interview — questions are sent in writing, and the person responds in writing. Common in journalism and research.

An interview can also be:

  • One-on-one — one interviewer, one interviewee.
  • Panel interview — multiple interviewers questioning one person at the same time.
  • Group interview — multiple candidates are interviewed together.

The noun "interview" captures the whole event — from the moment it begins to the moment it ends. So you can say:

  • "I have an interview tomorrow." (a scheduled event in the future)
  • "The interview lasted two hours." (a completed event)
  • "The interview was published in the newspaper." (a recorded or printed result)
  • "She gave an interview to the BBC." (the act of participating in one)
  • "He got the job after three rounds of interviews." (multiple instances)

An interview almost always leads to something. It might lead to a hiring decision, a published article, a research finding, a legal document, or an admission offer. The interview is not the end — it is the means by which information or judgment is gathered to reach a conclusion.

An interview is distinct from a test or exam — those evaluate fixed, objective knowledge. An interview evaluates the whole person: how they think, speak, react, and present themselves. It is more subjective, more human, and often more revealing than a written test.

In short: an interview is a purposeful, structured conversation in which one person questions another to gather information, make a judgment, or produce content — and it can happen in professional, journalistic, academic, medical, or legal settings.
